channel.description: Recent content in DevOps on DAWN's Blog

item.title: Harbor Active-Standby Deployment: From Installation to HTTPS and Replication
item.description: Complete guide to deploying Harbor enterprise Docker registry with active-standby architecture, HTTP/HTTPS modes, self-signed certificates, and cross-host replication.

item.title: RC Resources Do Not Support Declarative Updates
item.description: Hands-on verification of RC resources not supporting declarative updates: modifying the RC Pod image template, observing that running Pods do not update after kubectl apply, verifying that old Pods must be manually deleted to trigger new template recreation, and noting the risks of deleting all Pods directly in production.

item.title: K8S Pod Port Exposure and SVC Multi-Port Mapping in Practice: hostPort, Multi-Port Mapping and targetPort Name Matching
item.description: This article covers two things in K8S: exposing Pod ports and mapping multiple ports on a SVC. The first half uses hostPort to map container port 80 straight to 8888 on the node hosting the Pod, so external traffic reaches the container without going through a SVC; the access test from Windows succeeds, and hostPort is compared against NodePort (hostPort only works on the Pod’s node and its address follows the Pod when it moves, while NodePort is a Service that opens the same port on every node so movement does not affect access). The second half writes a Pod exposing both 80/TCP and 53/UDP, maps both through a SVC, inspects the PORT(S) column and the describe TargetPort/Endpoints, and finally patches targetPort to match by port name, verifying that the SVC keeps tracking the endpoint as long as the name is unchanged even if the container port number changes.

item.title: K8S Namespace Management in Practice: Imperative and Declarative Management, Cross-Namespace Service Access
item.description: This article walks through K8S namespace management. It starts with what namespaces do and how to tell namespaced from cluster-scoped resources (the NAMESPACED column of kubectl api-resources). Then it creates, lists, labels and deletes namespaces with imperative commands, and creates a Pod named xiuxian-v1 in both default and dawn to demonstrate isolation and the cascade delete that happens when a namespace is removed. Next it switches to declarative management: export a YAML from an existing resource and subtract from it, then apply to create a labeled namespace. Finally it puts MySQL in dawn and WordPress in kube-public, connects them using the cross-namespace short form db-svc.dawn, and lists the three ways to write a cross-namespace A record with the measured results.

item.title: K8S Pod DNS Policy and hostNetwork in Practice: A dnsPolicy Comparison
item.description: This article uses a control experiment to explain how a K8S Pod’s dnsPolicy interacts with hostNetwork. The test Pod sets hostNetwork: true and explicitly sets dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet; inside the container /etc/resolv.conf points at the cluster CoreDNS and carries the svc search domains, so db-svc, kubernetes and kube-dns all resolve. The control Pod only enables hostNetwork and leaves dnsPolicy at its ClusterFirst default; resolv.conf becomes the node’s own DNS with no search domains, and db-svc fails to resolve outright. Conclusion: once a Pod uses the host network, you must set dnsPolicy to ClusterFirstWithHostNet.

item.title: K8S in Practice: WordPress Deployment, NFS Persistence and CoreDNS Name Resolution
item.description: This article deploys WordPress on a K8S cluster and evolves it through three versions. v1 gets the basic chain working with ReplicationControllers and Services: MySQL RC to SVC ClusterIP with a pinned VIP, to WordPress RC, to SVC NodePort, finishing the installer in a browser; scaling WordPress to 3 replicas then exposes the data inconsistency caused by the lack of persistence. v2 introduces NFS shared storage so both MySQL data and the WordPress uploads directory land on NFS — after deleting the RC and letting it rebuild 3 fresh Pods, the marker files are still there, proving all replicas share the same data. v3 deploys the CoreDNS add-on so WordPress reaches the database by SVC name, and validates cluster DNS resolution three ways: from the manifests, by pinging SVC names inside a Pod, and with dig A-record lookups.

item.title: K8S Replica Control and Service Discovery in Practice: RC, ClusterIP and NodePort
item.description: This article works through replica control and service discovery in K8S. A ReplicationController declares 3 replicas; we verify its self-healing (deleting a Pod is automatically replenished) and that deleting the RC cascades to clean up the Pods it manages. Then a ClusterIP Service gives the 3 Pods spread across two nodes a single fixed entry point; with each Pod’s nginx returning its own Pod name, five consecutive requests reveal round-robin load balancing. Finally a NodePort Service exposes the workload on port 30080 of every node, reachable from outside the cluster and load balanced the same way.

item.title: K8S Troubleshooting Trio in Practice: kubectl explain, cp and logs
item.description: This article covers the three commands I reach for most when troubleshooting K8S. First build a troubleshooting test image that exits immediately, then use kubectl explain to read the OpenAPI Schema straight from the API Server and find out where a field belongs (no internet needed). Next, override the image’s default CMD with command + args in the Pod definition so a one-shot container stays running and can be inspected with exec. Finally, kubectl cp copies files both ways between the host and a Pod (config in, logs out), and kubectl logs is the first thing to check when a Pod misbehaves — it is how you track down CrashLoopBackOff.

item.title: K8S Volumes in Practice: emptyDir, hostPath and NFS
item.description: This article puts three K8S volume types to work. emptyDir is tied to the Pod lifecycle — a multi-container Pod shows both containers seeing the same data when the volume is mounted into each. hostPath mounts a host directory directly into the Pod; using Elasticsearch 7.17.16, indices survive deleting and recreating the Pod, proving single-node persistence. NFS solves cross-node sharing: configure nfs-kernel-server on the master, install nfs-common on all three nodes, deploy MySQL 8.3.0, write test data, then drift the Pod from worker01 to worker02 with the data fully intact. It closes with the selection rule: emptyDir for sharing inside a Pod, hostPath for single-node persistence, NFS (or distributed storage) when the workload must move across nodes.

item.title: K8S Core Resource Management and Pod Basics in Practice: Manifests, Multi-Container Pods, Labels and hostNetwork
item.description: This article walks through K8S core resource management and Pod basics. It starts with a cheat sheet of common resource short names and a kubectl api-resources overview, then covers routine health checks (worker node list, master components, the flannel interface and the cni0/flannel.1 virtual interfaces on each node). Next it writes single-container and multi-container Pod manifests, compares kubectl create with apply, and uses kubectl exec to enter a specific container. It then explains the difference between the declarative and imperative APIs, label create/read/update/delete plus filtering and deleting resources by label, and kubectl describe for resource details. Finally it demonstrates hostNetwork mode so a Pod shares the host network, and cleans up the lab environment.

item.title: K8S kubeadm Cluster Deployment in Practice: Harbor with a Self-Built CA and Flannel CNI
item.description: This hands-on guide builds a K8S kubeadm cluster (v1.23.17, 1 master + 2 workers, 3 nodes in total) from scratch. First install Docker on the harbor node and deploy a Harbor image registry (self-built CA issues the HTTPS certificate, harbor.yml enables port 443). Then install Docker on the three K8S nodes, configure /etc/hosts and the Docker client certificate, and verify docker login against Harbor successfully. Next prepare the nodes (disable swap, check product_uuid, configure iptables bridge traffic and the Aliyun apt repo, and install kubeadm/kubelet/kubectl), run kubeadm init on the master, configure kubeconfig, join the worker nodes, and finally deploy the Flannel CNI plugin so all three nodes become Ready, and verify cross-node Pod connectivity with curl.

item.title: Deploying containerd Runtime and Managing with runc/ctr in Practice
item.description: This hands-on walkthrough first uninstalls the Docker binaries on the docker02 node, then deploys the containerd 1.7.20 runtime (extracting cri-containerd-cni, installing the systemd unit, and editing config.toml to enable SystemdCgroup and replace the sandbox_image), and installs runc 1.1.12 along with the ctr client. It then demonstrates the full ctr workflow: pulling and tagging images, creating/starting/pausing/resuming/removing containers, namespace management, and pushing to and pulling from the docker01 Harbor (HTTP, non-TLS).

item.title: Harbor HTTPS Deployment with a Self-Signed Certificate
item.description: This hands-on walkthrough configures Harbor with HTTPS using a self-signed certificate. We create the certificate directory, generate a self-signed certificate with openssl (domain harbor.dawn.com, SAN covering both DNS and IP 11.0.1.122), edit harbor.yml to enable HTTPS on port 443, and reinstall with install.sh. Finally we use ss and curl to confirm that port 80 is automatically redirected to 443 and the WebUI is accessible. Self-signed certificates require client trust; in production, use a certificate issued by an official CA to avoid warnings.

item.title: Harbor High Availability: Implementing VIP Failover with keepalived
item.description: This hands-on walkthrough builds a Harbor high-availability solution using keepalived for VIP failover. keepalived is installed on docker01 and docker02, a port-check script is created, and a VRRP instance sharing the virtual IP 11.0.1.250 is configured (docker01 as MASTER with priority 100, docker02 as BACKUP with priority 90). After verifying the VIP currently points to docker01’s Harbor, keepalived on docker01 is stopped manually to observe the VIP drift to docker02 and the Harbor service switch, proving the keepalived HA scheme works.

item.title: Migrating Images from docker registry to Harbor and Syncing Between Two Harbors
item.description: This hands-on walkthrough migrates images from a docker registry into a Harbor registry and syncs images between two Harbor instances. Part 1 uses Harbor’s pull replication rule to sync the dawn-games/** images from the registry into a local Harbor project. Part 2 deploys Harbor on both the docker01 and docker02 nodes, then configures a Harbor-to-Harbor pull-mode replication rule to achieve two-Harbor image sync, finally modifying the client daemon.json and verifying.

item.title: Building a Custom Image Without a Base Image: Using scratch
item.description: scratch is a reserved name in Docker; when used as the base image in FROM it means no image is referenced, building a minimal image that contains only its own rootfs from scratch. This hands-on walkthrough downloads a third-party busybox root filesystem, injects a custom /etc/os-release, repackages it, writes a FROM scratch Dockerfile and docker-compose, builds and pushes the image to a Harbor registry, then pulls it from another host, starts the container, and verifies os-release and networking.

item.title: Hands-on with Private Image Registries: docker registry and VMware Harbor
item.description: Build two private image registries from scratch: first use the lightweight docker registry to complete image deployment, push, pull, and delete (including manually deleting metadata + GC to reclaim storage); then deploy the enterprise-grade VMware Harbor (HTTP mode), demonstrating hosts resolution, insecure-registries configuration, creating a project, three docker login methods, and the full image push/pull/delete flow; finally summarize the differences between registry and Harbor in size, deployment, WebUI, project management, deletion, and use cases with a comparison table.

item.title: Building Multi-Service Images and Starting Containers with docker-compose
item.description: Through a docker-compose case, demonstrate how to use a single YAML file to orchestrate image builds and container management for two HTML5 game services (doudizhu and motuo): write the compose file (build context + each service’s Dockerfile) together with nginx virtual hosts and a startup script, use docker-compose build to compile both images in one go, up -d to start in the background, ps/stop/start/restart/down to manage the lifecycle, then configure a fixed port with restart: always and a random port and verify access and the restart policy, and finally provide a reference table of common commands.

item.title: Hands-on with Multi-Stage Dockerfile Builds
item.description: Demonstrate how multi-stage builds (Multi-Stage Build) drastically shrink Docker image size: Part 1 builds v3.0 with three FROM stages (xixi/haha/final); the 24MB/2048MB large files generated by the first two stages do not enter the final image, which only COPYs two small logs (7.8MB). Part 2 uses Golang as an example: stage one compiles the hello binary with the Go SDK, stage two only COPYs the binary with COPY –from=0, yielding v3.2 at just 9.71MB versus 259MB for the single-stage v3.1, proving the slim multi-stage image is fully usable.

item.title: Hands-on with the Dockerfile ONBUILD Instruction
item.description: Use the You_Jump_I_Jump game image to demonstrate the Dockerfile ONBUILD instruction: understand its delayed-trigger mechanism (the defined instructions are not executed when the current image is built; they are only triggered automatically when another image uses this image as its base), write a base image Dockerfile containing two ONBUILD instructions (RUN to create directories/logs, LABEL to add the blog URL) and a child image Dockerfile, then after building v2.19/v2.20 compare OnBuild and Labels with docker inspect and compare the filesystem differences with containers, and finally explain how to use -f to specify multiple Dockerfiles to build different images.

item.title: Dockerfile: Running Containers as a Non-Root User (USER Instruction)
item.description: Use the Space Huggers game to demonstrate how to run a container as the non-root user dawn (uid 2025) with the Dockerfile USER instruction: first understand the directory/file ownership adjustments needed for nginx to run as a non-root user, then write the Dockerfile (chown system directories before switching to USER dawn), the nginx config (user dawn), and the startup script (nginx in background + tail to block), build the image and verify the process user, container configuration, access and health status, and finally compare the permission boundary where a non-root user can start nginx but cannot start sshd.

item.title: Dockerfile Core Instructions in Practice: WORKDIR/EXPOSE/VOLUME, ENV/ARG, HEALTHCHECK, ENTRYPOINT
item.description: Use 4 web games to demonstrate 7 core Dockerfile instructions in full: the working directory, port exposure and persistence effects of WORKDIR/EXPOSE/VOLUME; the difference between ENV and ARG at build time vs. run time and how to override them; the HEALTHCHECK health-status transitions; and the non-overridable/overridable distinction between ENTRYPOINT and CMD plus the argument-passing mechanism.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Tag Images with MAINTAINER and LABEL, and Inspect Metadata
item.description: Using a real dawn-games image, demonstrate writing author/school/email metadata into the Dockerfile with the deprecated MAINTAINER and the officially recommended LABEL, then reading .Author and .Config.Labels back with docker image inspect -f to verify, and starting the container with –network host to access over the host network. Includes a screenshot.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Dockerfile Optimization Tips and Container Startup Techniques
item.description: A practical roundup of Docker efficiency tips: build-side image layer caching (Using cache) and .dockerignore to shrink a 1GB build context to <del>1.6MB; runtime tricks docker exec -w for the working directory, anonymous volume host paths (/var/lib/docker/volumes/<hash>/_data), and -p :80 random port mapping (32768</del>60999).

item.title: Docker in Practice: Building Docker Images Manually and Automatically with a Dockerfile
item.description: Build the same nginx game image manually from three base images - CentOS, Ubuntu and Alpine - and commit it with docker commit (236MB / 215MB / 9.41MB), then rebuild it with a Dockerfile, and summarize the three drawbacks of the manual approach: oversized images, tedious startup-command changes, and no build cache.

item.title: Docker in Practice: The Difference Between docker exec and docker attach
item.description: Use docker top to compare process trees and see the essential difference between docker exec and docker attach: exec spawns a new process inside the container, while attach only connects your local stdin/stdout/stderr to the container’s running main process. Also shows how to detach from attach with ctrl+p then ctrl+q without terminating the container.

item.title: Docker in Practice: A Detailed Look at Container States — Up / Exited / Created / Paused
item.description: Reproduce how each of the four container states shown by docker ps is produced — Up, Exited (exit-code semantics: 0 = normal, 137 = SIGKILL), Created (created but not started), and Paused (suspended from serving, and unlike restart it does not reset the status timer).

item.title: Docker in Practice: Linux Namespace Network Isolation and CGroup Resource Limits
item.description: Build a Linux network namespace by hand with ip netns, connect it to the outside world through a veth pair and NAT, then see how Docker containers share a net namespace; finally stress CPU and memory under cgroup v2 limits and reproduce an OOM kill, tying together the two low-level mechanisms behind containers: isolation (Namespace) and limits (CGroup).

item.title: Docker in Practice: Overlay Cross-Host Container Networking with a WordPress Case
item.description: Initialize a Swarm cluster on two Docker hosts, create the attachable overlay network dawn-overlay, demonstrate cross-host container communication by IP and container name, verify Internet egress via docker_gwbridge, observe encapsulation by capturing VXLAN (UDP 4789) packets, and finish with a cross-host WordPress deployment.

item.title: Docker in Practice: macvlan for Cross-Host Container Networking
item.description: Create same-subnet custom networks with the macvlan driver on two Docker hosts and demonstrate cross-host Layer-2 container connectivity; also cover the fix for macvlan’s default inability to reach the host or the Internet, and finish with a multi-node WordPress deployment.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Deploying Zabbix Monitoring and a WordPress App with Docker
item.description: On a single host with a custom network, deploy the Zabbix stack (MySQL + Java gateway + Server + Web) and a WordPress app with docker run, including port mapping and persistent volumes.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Single-Host Network Types and Container Communication Options
item.description: Docker single-host networking: the five network types none, bridge, host, container and custom, with hands-on examples, plus three container-to-container communication options - /etc/hosts resolution, –link, and custom networks (including create, inspect, prune, custom subnets and manual IP assignment).

item.title: Docker in Practice: Container Isolation and Cross-Network Communication with Multiple Bridge Networks
item.description: Using two custom Bridge networks, xixi and haha, this walkthrough demonstrates Docker’s default network isolation mechanism and shows how docker network connect/disconnect lets a container join or leave a network at runtime to achieve cross-network container communication.

item.title: Docker in Practice: OverlayFS Union Mounts and the Storage Driver Explained
item.description: How the Docker OverlayFS storage driver works: the lower/upper/work directories and the LowerDir/Upperdir/MergedDir layers (including the init layer), and copy-on-write into the read-write layer; then a manual mount -t overlay demo of layering and read-only behavior, and finally docker run to confirm that a container is backed by overlay2.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Hand-Building a Minimal Container Root with chroot to Understand What a Container Is
item.description: Without Docker commands, use chroot to hand-build a minimal container root from scratch (copying bash and its dynamic-library chain) to feel filesystem isolation; then show two independent roots make processes/data invisible to each other, and finally chroot into a real container’s overlay2 merged filesystem to fix files and read logs.

item.title: Docker in Practice: WordPress Multi-Node Deployment and Persistence Verification
item.description: Deploy WordPress with Docker across two nodes (database and web separated), persist data with named volumes, then delete and recreate the containers to verify the published blog is not lost.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Building a Multi-Game Image with Dockerfile and ADD Auto-Extraction
item.description: Copy the static files of two games (Gold Miner and Flappy Bird) out of an old all-in-one image dawn-games-dawn:v0.6 using a staging container, pack each into a tar.gz, then let the Dockerfile ADD instruction auto-extract them into an Alpine+nginx container at build time; finally build the image, start the container and visit both games by domain — plus the key difference between ADD and COPY: ADD auto-extracts tar.gz.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Container Data Persistence - bind Mounts and Volumes
item.description: Mount host paths into containers with -v, share one mount point across containers, attach several mount points to a single container and set rw/ro permissions, then cover the whole docker volume workflow: create, inspect, delete, anonymous volumes and re-mounting a running container.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Container Lifecycle Management - Start, Stop and Restart Policies
item.description: Walk through container lifecycle management: docker stop, start and restart plus custom startup commands, then the five restart policies - create five containers with different policies, kill them with kill -9 to compare restart counters, and see which ones come back after dockerd restarts.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Deploying Applications - Tomcat / MySQL / WordPress / ELK
item.description: Deploy real applications with docker run: Tomcat, MySQL (including bulk 20-instance startup and multi-instance exposure), WordPress and the ElasticSearch + Kibana stack, with port mapping, persistent volumes and password/token setup.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Inspecting Container PID, ID and Network Info with inspect
item.description: Use docker container inspect -f with Go templates to pull a container’s PID, ID, IP address, gateway and MAC address.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Nginx Load Balancing and Container Traffic Distribution
item.description: Run an lb container plus two web containers, edit the Nginx default.conf on lb to reverse-proxy to web01/web02, then curl the lb 10 times to see the traffic alternate between the two backends.

item.title: Docker in Practice: The Full Flow of Pulling an Image and Starting a Container
item.description: Walk through Docker’s three core objects in order — image registry, image, container: inspect the local registry list, pull an image from a remote registry, start a container, and run an access test.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Passing and Inspecting Environment Variables in Containers
item.description: How to pass environment variables into a container with -e and how to inspect them afterwards with docker exec <container> env.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Image Migration - Offline save/load Transfer and Tagging
item.description: Export an image with docker save, transfer it offline over SSH, verify integrity with md5sum, then import it with docker load and re-tag it. Shows that save/load preserves the IMAGE ID, how to export multiple images at once, two import forms, and two ways to batch-delete images.

item.title: Docker in Practice: How Port Mapping Works - From the veth NIC to iptables DNAT
item.description: Observe how Docker maps a container port to the host: from the veth NIC and the docker0 bridge, to the iptables DNAT rules and the net.ipv4.ip_forward kernel switch that makes external access work.

item.title: Docker in Practice: Common Container Commands and exec Operations
item.description: A roundup of everyday container commands (list/remove/rename containers, follow logs with -f/–since/–until, copy files with docker cp) plus running commands inside a running container with docker exec, including the gotcha that the target command must exist in the image.

item.title: Docker Installation in Practice: Binary Deployment and One-Click Script Deployment
item.description: Install Docker three ways: via the apt package manager, from official static binaries (download/extract/copy/start), and with an automation script (install and uninstall). Also covers how to cleanly remove the binary install.

item.title: SonarQube in Practice: Self-hosted Deployment, Token Setup, and Code Quality Scanning
item.description: A complete hands-on SonarQube self-hosting guide: JDK 8 and MySQL 5.6 setup, extracting SonarQube with plugins, running as a non-root user, web token configuration, and scanning code with the sonar-scanner client.

item.title: Jenkins in Practice: Self-hosted Deployment, Plugin Setup, and GitLab-Driven CI
item.description: A complete hands-on Jenkins self-hosting guide: RPM install of JDK and Jenkins, running as root, offline plugin install, and wiring GitLab SSH keyless access with webhook-triggered CI builds.

item.title: GitLab in Practice: Self-hosted Deployment, SSH Keyless Access, and Repository Management
item.description: A complete hands-on guide to self-hosting GitLab: RPM install, components, common commands, web UI setup, SSH keyless access, and multi-user collaboration.

item.title: Git in Practice: Installation, Essential Commands, and Branch Management
item.description: A hands-on Git walkthrough covering installation, everyday commands, branch workflows, and conflict resolution.
